# On the Art of Noticing

There is a particular quality of light that comes through a window on a late October afternoon—thin, ambered, almost apologetic, as though the sun knows it has been extravagant all summer and is now rationing itself. I noticed it first in my grandmother's kitchen when I was seven, sitting at the linoleum table with a glass of milk and a cookie I was not supposed to have before dinner. The light fell across the counter in a long parallelogram, catching the dust motes that drifted like tiny, aimless planets. I remember thinking—not in words, but in that pre-verbal way children have of receiving information directly into their bones—that this was a thing worth paying attention to. It was the first time I can recall noticing something not because it was loud or bright or demanded my attention, but because it was quiet and the noticing itself felt like a small act of creation.

I have been thinking about that moment for years now, and I have come to believe it holds the key to something important. We live in an age that has declared war on the unremarkable. Every feed, every notification, every headline is engineered to seize the amygdala and not let go. We are bombarded with the extraordinary, the urgent, the outrageous—and in the process, we lose our capacity for the ordinary, which is where most of life actually happens. The dust motes in the afternoon light are still there. We have simply stopped seeing them.

I want to write about the art of noticing. Not as a self-help prescription—I am suspicious of anything that promises to optimize my attention for productivity—but as a way of being in the world that feels increasingly endangered and increasingly necessary. Noticing is not a skill we cultivate so we can do more; it is a practice we cultivate so we can *be* more. It is the difference between walking through a forest while thinking about your grocery list and walking through a forest while walking through a forest.

The problem is that noticing has become countercultural. We are trained from childhood to look past things. The classroom rewards the answer, not the question. The workplace rewards the outcome, not the process. The social media feed rewards the performance, not the moment. Even our leisure is often organized around consumption—we binge, we scroll, we move through content like a machine that needs to be fed. The idea of simply sitting with something, letting it reveal itself slowly, has become almost radical.

But here is what I have learned: the things worth noticing usually do not announce themselves. They accumulate. They wait. They require a certain kind of patience that feels almost like a form of prayer.

My father was a carpenter, and he used to say that the best wood is the wood you almost throw away. He would stand in the lumberyard for what felt like hours, running his hand along the grain, turning over boards that looked to me like ordinary planks and seeing something I could not. He would notice the way the fiber tightened around a knot, the subtle variation in color that signaled a particular kind of stress, the smell of the wood—did it smell sharp, or sweet, or slightly sour? He was not looking for perfection. He was looking for character. He was looking for the story the wood had been telling while it grew.

I used to think this was just a carpenter's eccentricity, a professional tic. But now I understand that he was practicing something larger. He was training himself to see what other people overlooked, to find value in what appeared to be flaws. And I think this is what noticing really is: it is the ability to see the story in things. It is understanding that every object, every person, every moment is the accumulated record of its own becoming. The crack in the sidewalk is not just a crack; it is the story of frost and roots and the slow insistence of time. The stranger on the bus is not just a stranger; they are carrying a lifetime of experiences that have shaped the way they hold their jaw and the particular rhythm of their breathing.

This is not sentimentality. It is attention. And attention, as Simone Weil said, is the rarest and purest form of generosity.

I remember a period in my life when I was profoundly unhappy—not in a dramatic, crisis way, but in the low-grade, chronic way that feels almost worse because it lacks a clear cause. I was working a job I did not care about, living in a city I did not love, and I had developed the habit of moving through my days without actually being present in them. I was a ghost in my own life. I ate without tasting, walked without seeing, listened without hearing. The world had become a blur, and I had become a blur along with it.

What broke the spell was something almost embarrassingly small. I had stopped at a traffic light on my way home from work, and I happened to look down at the sidewalk. There was a dandelion growing in a crack in the concrete. It had pushed through a space that could not have been more than a millimeter wide, and it was blooming—not modestly, not apologetically, but with a kind of defiant, ridiculous yellow brightness. I remember feeling something crack open inside me. I remember thinking, *if this thing can do that, so can I*.

It sounds trite, I know. A dandelion in a crack in the sidewalk is the most clichéd metaphor for resilience in the book. But here is the thing: it wasn't a metaphor to me in that moment. It was a dandelion. It was actually there. And the fact that I had looked at it—really looked at it, for the first time in months—was the beginning of something.

I started noticing again. I started paying attention. And slowly, the world started coming back into focus.

I have a theory about why this works. I think that noticing is a relational act. It is not something we do to the world; it is something we do *with* the world. When we notice something, we enter into a relationship with it. We acknowledge its existence. We give it a small piece of our attention, and in return, it gives us a small piece of its reality. This is why being noticed feels so good—why someone remembering a small detail about you, or asking a follow-up question, or simply meeting your eyes with genuine interest, can feel like a form of love.

Kurt Vonnegut once said that the most important thing a person can do is to notice when something is beautiful. He was not talking about grand beauty—sunsets and masterpieces and the faces of the people we love. He was talking about the small, easily overlooked beauty of everyday life. The shape of a leaf. The sound of a hinge. The way someone's eyes crinkle when they are trying not to laugh. These are the things that make a life. These are the things we remember.

But we cannot remember what we do not notice. And we cannot notice what we do not slow down for.

This is, I think, the central problem of our age. We have traded the depth of the particular for the breadth of the general. We know a thousand things about the world but almost nothing about what is immediately in front of us. We can tell you the latest news from a country we have never visited but cannot tell you the name of our neighbor's dog. We have become experts at the distant and novices at the near.

Thoreau went to Walden Pond not to escape the world but to learn how to see it. He spent two years, two months, and two days in a cabin in the woods, and most of what he did was notice. He noticed the ice melting, the ants fighting, the owl crying, the pond freezing. He noticed the way the seasons moved through the landscape and through him. He noticed the cost of things—not just the dollar cost, but the life cost, the time cost, the attention cost. And he came back with a book that people have been reading for over a century and a half, not because it is about anything extraordinary, but because it is about the extraordinary nature of the ordinary.

I think we need more Thoreaus. Not people who retreat to cabins in the woods—most of us cannot do that, and anyway, the woods are full—but people who commit to noticing the world they actually live in. People who walk the same streets every day and find something new each time. People who eat the same breakfast and taste it each time. People who look at the people they love and actually see them, rather than seeing the idea of them they have constructed in their heads.

Noticing is not a passive act. It requires effort. It requires discipline. It requires the willingness to be bored, which is perhaps the hardest thing of all. When we are bored, we reach for our phones. We fill the silence. We distract ourselves. But boredom is often the doorway to noticing. It is only when we have exhausted the easy stimulations that we begin to see what is actually there.

I have been trying to practice this in my own life. It is harder than I expected. The world is designed to prevent it. Every app, every notification, every headline is a small hook trying to pull my attention away from whatever I am actually doing. And I am weak. I scroll. I click. I wander.

But I am getting better. I have started to notice the sound of my footsteps when I walk to work. I have started to notice the way the light changes over the course of a day. I have started to notice the particular way my wife hums when she is concentrating, the way the dog tilts his head when he is confused, the way the coffee smells when I grind the beans in the morning. These are tiny things. They are nothing. They are everything.

There is a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*, which translates roughly to "the pathos of things." It is the awareness of the impermanence of the world, the recognition that everything is fleeting and therefore precious. The cherry blossoms bloom for a week and then fall. We can choose to mourn that, or we can choose to notice it—to be present for the blooming, and present for the falling. Both are part of the same thing.

I think this is what noticing is ultimately about. It is not just about seeing the world more clearly. It is about accepting it. It is about recognizing that we are not separate from the world—that we are made of the same stuff, subject to the same forces, moving through the same time. When I notice the dust motes in the afternoon light, I am noticing myself. When I notice the dandelion in the crack, I am noticing my own capacity to persist. When I notice the people I love, I am noticing the ways they have shaped me and the ways I have shaped them.

This is not a small thing. It is, in fact, the only thing.

I have been thinking about my grandmother again. She died when I was fifteen, and I remember very little about her now—her voice, her face, the way she laughed. But I remember the kitchen. I remember the linoleum table and the glass of milk and the parallelogram of light. I remember her hands, which were always busy, and the way she would pause in the middle of whatever she was doing to look out the window. She was not looking at anything in particular, I think. She was just looking. She was giving the world her attention, and the world was giving her something back.

I think that is the best thing we can do with our lives. It is not to achieve great things or accumulate great wealth or become great people. It is to pay attention. It is to notice. It is to sit in the kitchen and watch the light move across the counter and understand that this, too, is a miracle—ordinary, unremarkable, and utterly, completely, impossibly real.

The light is fading now. It is late afternoon, and the amber is turning to gold, and the gold is turning to gray. The dust motes are still there, but they are harder to see. I could get up and turn on a lamp, and I probably will in a moment. But for now, I am going to sit here and watch. I am going to notice. I am going to let the world be what it is, and I am going to be what I am, and I am going to find out what happens when I stop trying to be anywhere else.

It is not much, this practice. It is not a solution to the problems of the world. It will not make me happier, exactly, or more successful, or more important. But it will make me more awake. And on the days when I am awake—the days when the light finds me, and I find it—I feel something that I can only describe as gratitude. Not for anything in particular. Just gratitude, period. The gratitude of being here, in this moment, taking it in.

That seems like a good place to stop. The light is almost gone. The kitchen is dark. And somewhere, a dandelion is pushing through a crack in the sidewalk, waiting to be seen.
